body:
What is history?

History is the study of the human past. It examines how people lived, organised their societies, produced food, traded, developed beliefs, established kingdoms and experienced changes over time. Historical knowledge is based on evidence left behind by people and societies.

We know about the past through objects, buildings, written records, accounts of travellers and other surviving evidence. A historical account becomes more reliable when its claims are supported by suitable sources.

A historical source is an object, document, inscription, account or other surviving evidence that provides information about the past.

Why are different kinds of sources necessary?

Different sources answer different questions. A stone tool can help us understand the activities of early humans. The remains of a house can reveal aspects of settlement and construction. An inscription may record an order issued by a ruler. A coin can provide information about political authority, exchange or religious symbols.

No single type of source provides a complete account of a society. Written records often describe rulers, religious institutions and important events more extensively than the everyday lives of ordinary people. Material remains can therefore reveal aspects of history that written records do not describe.

Major categories of historical sources

Source categoryExamplesInformation commonly obtained
Archaeological remainsTools, pottery, buildings, burials, ornamentsSettlement, technology, food, crafts and daily life
InscriptionsWriting on rocks, pillars and copper platesRoyal orders, donations, public works and political claims
CoinsPunch-marked, copper, silver and gold coinsRulers, exchange, symbols and monetary activity
Literary sourcesReligious texts, poems, chronicles and manuscriptsBeliefs, ideas, social practices and accounts of events
Travellers' accountsDescriptions written by visitorsObservations about places, institutions and society

These categories can overlap. A coin is a material object, but its inscription can also provide written evidence. A copper-plate land grant is an archaeological object as well as an inscription. The classification depends partly on the type of information being studied.

Evidence and historical claims

A historical claim must be supported by evidence that is relevant to it. For example, the remains of drains at Mohenjodaro support the conclusion that the city possessed a drainage system. They do not, by themselves, establish the name of the city's ruler.

Similarly, an inscription stating that a king ordered a public work establishes that the order was recorded. Whether every part of the work was completed may require additional evidence.

Primary and secondary sources

A primary source comes directly from the period or activity being studied. Examples include an ancient coin, a contemporary inscription and the remains of a building. A secondary source is a later account or explanation based on earlier evidence, such as a modern history textbook.

The distinction depends on the historical question. A medieval chronicle is a primary source for understanding how its author described contemporary events, but it may be a later account of events that occurred centuries before the author lived.

Who studies these sources?

  • Historians study and interpret evidence to reconstruct human history.
  • Archaeologists study material remains such as structures, pottery, tools and burials.
  • Epigraphists study inscriptions.
  • Numismatists study coins.

The existence of a source and the truth of every claim made in that source are different matters. A royal inscription is evidence of what the ruler recorded; its claims must be understood in context.

Prelims focus

  • History studies the human past using surviving evidence.
  • Archaeology deals principally with material remains.
  • Epigraphy is the study of inscriptions.
  • Numismatics is the study of coins.
  • An inscription or coin may belong to more than one source category.
  • Trap: A written statement is not automatically proof that everything described in it happened exactly as stated.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 1, pp. 4–7; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 4, pp. 66–68; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, pp. 46–49.]

pictures.caption: Objects used in everyday life can become important sources of historical evidence.

title: How Historians Reconstruct the Past

body:
Why is chronology important?

Chronology is the arrangement of events in the order in which they occurred. It helps us distinguish earlier events from later ones, identify whether developments were contemporary and understand the sequence of historical change.

Historical dates may identify a particular year, but many changes took place gradually. The development of agriculture, the growth of cities and the spread of cultural practices cannot always be assigned to a single exact year.

BCE and CE

The commonly used historical dating system divides years into BCE and CE.

  • BCE means Before Common Era. It is equivalent to the older designation BC, meaning Before Christ.
  • CE means Common Era. It corresponds to the older designation AD, from the Latin expression Anno Domini.

The change from BC and AD to BCE and CE changes the terminology, not the numbering of years. Thus, 250 BCE corresponds to 250 BC, and 2026 CE corresponds to AD 2026.

How years are counted

Within the BCE period, years are counted backward towards the beginning of the Common Era. Therefore, 500 BCE is earlier than 250 BCE.

Within the CE period, years move forward. Therefore, 500 CE is later than 250 CE.

The absence of year 0

The conventional BCE–CE historical calendar has no year 0. The year immediately following 1 BCE is 1 CE.

When calculating the elapsed years between a BCE date and a CE date, add the 2 year numbers and subtract 1.

Calculating elapsed years

The time from 200 BCE to 200 CE is \(200+200-1=399\) years.

The time from 2 BCE to 2 CE is \(2+2-1=3\) years.

For 2 dates within the same era, subtract the smaller year number from the larger one. For example, 300 BCE to 200 BCE represents an interval of 100 years.

Centuries and millennia

A century contains 100 years, while a millennium contains 1000 years. The historical numbering of centuries begins with year 1, not year 0.

PeriodYears included
1st century CE1–100 CE
4th century CE301–400 CE
5th century CE401–500 CE
21st century CE2001–2100 CE
1st century BCE100–1 BCE
3rd century BCE300–201 BCE
1st millennium BCE1000–1 BCE
1st millennium CE1–1000 CE

The year 400 BCE belongs to the 4th century BCE, while 400 CE belongs to the 4th century CE. The year 401 CE begins the 5th century CE.

Approximate dates and other expressions

  • c. is an abbreviation of circa, meaning approximately. The expression c. 2600 BCE does not claim an exact date.
  • BP means Before Present. It is used in some discussions of the distant past and should not be treated as identical to BCE without knowing its reference point; in radiocarbon dating, this is conventionally 1950 CE.
  • Decade means a period of 10 years.
  • Regnal year means a year counted from a ruler's accession or another stated starting point of the reign. It is not automatically a CE date.

Indian historical records may employ different eras and calendars. When an inscription gives a year according to a particular era, the era must be identified before the date can be expressed in BCE or CE.

Prelims focus

  • BCE corresponds to BC; CE corresponds to AD.
  • Within BCE, 600 BCE precedes 300 BCE.
  • 1 BCE is immediately followed by 1 CE; there is no year 0.
  • The 3rd century BCE extends from 300 BCE to 201 BCE.
  • The 21st century CE extends from 2001 CE to 2100 CE.
  • Trap: 200 BCE to 200 CE is an interval of 399 years, not 400 years.

[Sources: NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 4, pp. 61–65; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 1, pp. 7–8.]

pictures.caption: There is no year 0 between 1 BCE and 1 CE.

title: Understanding BCE, CE, Centuries and Historical Dates

body:
Historical periods help organise long stretches of time

Indian history covers many thousands of years. Dividing this long span into periods makes it easier to identify major changes in settlement, technology, political organisation and cultural life.

The terms prehistoric, protohistoric, ancient and medieval describe different ways of understanding the past. Their boundaries are not always exact, and developments did not begin everywhere in India at the same time.

Prehistory, protohistory and history

Prehistory

Prehistory generally refers to periods for which written records are not available. Information about the people of these periods comes mainly from material remains such as stone tools, shelters, pottery, bones and other objects.

The prehistoric sequence is commonly discussed through the Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic periods.

  • Palaeolithic: the Old Stone Age, associated with early stone tools and hunting-gathering societies.
  • Mesolithic: the Middle Stone Age, associated with developments in stone-tool traditions and forms of hunting and gathering.
  • Neolithic: the New Stone Age, associated in many regions with farming, animal domestication and more settled living.

These stages did not replace one another simultaneously across the subcontinent. Hunting, gathering, cultivation and herding could continue alongside one another.

Chalcolithic and Bronze Age developments

The term Chalcolithic refers to the use of copper alongside stone tools. Bronze, an alloy based mainly on copper and tin, became important in the Bronze Age. These terms identify material and technological traditions rather than a single political period shared by every region.

Protohistory and the Harappan civilisation

Protohistory is often used for societies whose written records cannot yet be read or whose history must be reconstructed largely through archaeological and related evidence. The Harappan civilisation is a major Indian example because its seals bear signs of an undeciphered script.

The Mature Harappan period is conventionally dated to approximately 2600–1900 BCE. Its cities, buildings, seals, weights, pottery and crafts provide extensive evidence, even though the inscriptions have not been deciphered.

Major chronological landmarks

Several broad chronological markers are especially useful for placing events and sources in the correct order.

Early Vedic and early historic developments

The Rigveda is a major source for early Vedic traditions. Its hymns were composed and transmitted orally during the 2nd millennium BCE. The date of composition and the date of a surviving manuscript copy are not necessarily the same.

From around the 6th century BCE, the rise of the mahajanapadas, the growth of towns and the increasing use of coinage became important developments in parts of the subcontinent.

Mauryan and Gupta periods

Chandragupta Maurya established the Mauryan Empire around 321 BCE. The inscriptions of his grandson Ashoka, who ruled in the 3rd century BCE, provide valuable contemporary evidence for the Mauryan period.

The Gupta period, particularly the 4th–6th centuries CE, is studied through inscriptions, coins, literature and other material remains.

Early medieval India

The term early medieval India is commonly applied to developments from approximately the 7th to 12th centuries CE. Regional kingdoms, land grants, inscriptions and literary records are important sources for this period.

These dates are broad conventions. Political and social changes unfolded differently across regions, and many institutions and practices continued from earlier periods.

Why periodisation must not be treated as an absolute division

History is often organised into ancient, medieval and modern periods. These are useful teaching categories, but they should not suggest that every earlier institution disappeared when a new period began.

In 1817, James Mill published A History of British India, dividing Indian history into Hindu, Muslim and British periods. This division is unsuitable as a complete account of Indian history because the religion of a ruler cannot describe the beliefs, social life and historical experiences of an entire population.

Chronological sequence identifies which events came earlier or later. Periodisation groups developments into broader periods. A period label is not necessarily the date of a single event.

Prelims focus

  • Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic are major prehistoric divisions.
  • Chalcolithic means the use of copper alongside stone.
  • The Mature Harappan period is dated approximately 2600–1900 BCE.
  • The rise of mahajanapadas is associated with the period from around the 6th century BCE.
  • Chandragupta Maurya established his empire around 321 BCE; Ashoka belongs to the 3rd century BCE.
  • Trap: Ancient, medieval and modern are broad divisions, not dates when every feature of society changed simultaneously.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapters 1–3 and 5; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Themes 1–2, pp. 1–3 and 28–33; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 1, pp. 12–13; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 1, pp. 3–4.]
